--- title: "Neural Posterior Estimation" description: "Train a neural network on simulations to approximate the posterior of any dataset generated by a model." categories: [Simulation-based inference, Neural Networks] order: 40 reading-time: true --- ## General Principles Like [Approximate Bayesian Computation](38.%20Approximate%20Bayesian%20Computation.qmd), Neural Posterior Estimation (NPE) performs Bayesian inference for models that can be simulated but whose likelihood is intractable. Instead of accepting or rejecting simulations, NPE *learns* the posterior: 1) Simulate many pairs $(\theta, x)$ from the model: $\theta$ from the prior, then a dataset $x$ given $\theta$. 2) Train a neural network $q_\phi(\theta \mid x)$, a [conditional density estimator 🛈]{#cde}, to predict the distribution of $\theta$ from the (summary statistics of the) data $x$. 3) Evaluate the trained network at the observed data: $q_\phi(\theta \mid x_{obs})$ approximates the posterior $p(\theta \mid x_{obs})$. Because every simulation is used (none is rejected), NPE typically needs far fewer simulations than ABC. And because the network has learned the posterior for *every* possible dataset, it is **amortized**: once trained, the posterior of a new dataset costs one forward pass, with no new simulations. ## Considerations ::: callout-note - The model is written as in any BF chapter; `m.npe()` uses it only as a simulator. As in ABC, the data are summarized with `summary_stats` (a function, or `"identity"`, `"moments"`, `"quantiles"`, `"robust"`). NPE copes with more statistics than ABC, since the network learns which ones matter. - Two density estimators are available through `estimator`: - `"mdn"` (default): a *mixture density network* [@bishop1994mixture], the posterior is a mixture of `n_components` multivariate Normal distributions whose weights, means and covariances are outputs of a neural network built with BF's BNN layers. - `"flow"`: a conditional *normalizing flow* [@dinh2017density], a chain of `n_layers` invertible transformations of a Normal distribution. More flexible for strongly non-Gaussian posteriors. - Parameters are learned in the unconstrained space of their prior support and transformed back, so constraints such as $\sigma > 0$ always hold. - A posterior estimated by NPE must be **checked for calibration**. `m.sbc_coverage()` simulates new $(\theta^*, x^*)$ pairs and measures how often $\theta^*$ falls in the $\alpha\%$ highest-posterior-density region: a calibrated posterior lies on the diagonal, an over-confident one below it [@hermans2022trust]. - With small simulation budgets, NPE posteriors tend to be over-confident; [Bayesian NPE](41.%20Bayesian%20Neural%20Posterior%20Estimation.qmd) addresses this. ::: ## Example Below is an example code snippet demonstrating *Neural Posterior Estimation* using the BayesForge (**BF**) package. As in the [ABC chapter](38.%20Approximate%20Bayesian%20Computation.qmd), we use the linear regression of height on weight of [chapter 1](1.%20Linear%20Regression%20for%20continuous%20variable.qmd) [@mcelreath2018statistical], whose exact posterior is available with MCMC, and the least-squares intercept, slope and residual standard deviation as (sufficient) summary statistics. NPE is trained on 20 000 simulated datasets; the trained network then gives the posterior of the observed data and, without retraining, of three new datasets. The *From scratch* tab writes the mixture density network as a BF model (BF priors on the weights, `m.bnn.layer_linear`, `m.bnn.layer_mixture_normal`) and trains it with `m.svi`; the *Built-in function* tab obtains the same result with `m.npe()`. A parameter-recovery study on the g-and-k distribution, whose likelihood is intractable, is available in the `Test/16.SBI/g-and-k` folder of the repository. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Python ::: {#d3dc2b56 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} from BayesForge import bf import jax import jax.numpy as jnp import numpyro import matplotlib.pyplot as plt # Setup device------------------------------------------------ m = bf(platform="cpu", rand_seed=0) # Import Data & Data Manipulation ------------------------------------------------ data_path = m.load.howell1(only_path=True) m.data(data_path, sep=";") m.df = m.df[m.df.age > 18] # Subset data to adults m.scale(["weight"]) # Normalize # Define model ------------------------------------------------ def model(weight, height): a = m.dist.normal(178, 20, name="a") b = m.dist.log_normal(0, 1, name="b") s = m.dist.uniform(0, 50, name="s") m.dist.normal(a + b * weight, s, obs=height) # Summary statistics ------------------------------------------------ weight = jnp.asarray(m.df.weight.values) height_obs = jnp.asarray(m.df.height.values) X = jnp.stack([jnp.ones_like(weight), weight], axis=1) def ols(height): """Least-squares intercept, slope and residual sd: sufficient for this model.""" coef = jnp.linalg.lstsq(X, height)[0] return jnp.array([coef[0], coef[1], jnp.std(height - X @ coef)]) # Three new datasets, simulated with known parameters (to test amortization) ---------- new_truths = [{"a": 150.0, "b": 4.0, "s": 4.0}, {"a": 160.0, "b": 7.0, "s": 6.0}, {"a": 170.0, "b": 2.0, "s": 8.0}] new_heights = [m.dist.normal(t["a"] + t["b"] * weight, t["s"], sample=True) for t in new_truths] # Reference: exact posterior with MCMC ------------------------------------------------ m.fit(model, progress_bar=False) nuts = dict(m.posteriors) howell = {"weight": weight, "height": height_obs} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` bf v 0.0.48 package loaded jax.local_device_count 32 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.panel-tabset} #### From scratch NPE written out step by step with BF functions only. Each line of the model becomes a BF draw with `sample=True` to build the training set. The network is itself a BF model: its weights are `m.dist.normal` priors, its layers are `m.bnn.layer_linear`, and its output layer `m.bnn.layer_mixture_normal` is the likelihood of the simulated parameters. Training is BF's stochastic variational inference (`m.svi`) with a point-mass guide (`AutoDelta`): the weights are set to their posterior mode, i.e. the network minimizes $-\log q(u \mid s)$ plus a small weight decay from the Normal priors, on mini-batches of 256 simulations (a subsampled `m.dist.plate`). Posterior draws are then predictions of the trained model (`m.sample`). ::: {#6828f89c .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} from numpyro.infer import Trace_ELBO from numpyro.infer.autoguide import AutoDelta from numpyro.infer.initialization import init_to_sample # 1. Training set: parameters from the priors, one simulated dataset each ------------ M = 20_000 a = m.dist.normal(178, 20, sample=True, shape=(M,)) b = m.dist.log_normal(0, 1, sample=True, shape=(M,)) s = m.dist.uniform(0, 50, sample=True, shape=(M,)) height = m.dist.normal(a[:, None] + b[:, None] * weight, s[:, None], sample=True) # (M, n_obs) stats = jax.vmap(ols)(height) # (M, 3) # 2. Unconstrained, standardised parameters and statistics --------------------------- # a is real, b > 0 -> log(b), s in (0, 50) -> logit(s / 50) u = jnp.stack([a, jnp.log(b), jax.scipy.special.logit(s / 50)], axis=1) u_mean, u_sd = u.mean(0), u.std(0) s_mean, s_sd = stats.mean(0), stats.std(0) un, sn = (u - u_mean) / u_sd, (stats - s_mean) / s_sd def to_params(u_std): """Standardised unconstrained draws -> dict of (a, b, s) on their natural scales.""" u = u_std * u_sd + u_mean return {"a": u[:, 0], "b": jnp.exp(u[:, 1]), "s": 50 * jax.nn.sigmoid(u[:, 2])} # 3. The network as a BF model: weight priors, BNN layers, mixture likelihood ------- D, K, H = 3, 5, 64 # parameters, mixture components, hidden units sizes = [3, H, H, m.bnn.mixture_normal_size(K, D)] # K * (1 + D + D(D+1)/2) outputs def npe_net(c, u=None, batch_size=None): params = [(m.dist.normal(0, 1 / jnp.sqrt(n_in), shape=(n_in, n_out), name=f"W{i}"), m.dist.normal(0, 1, shape=(n_out,), name=f"b{i}")) for i, (n_in, n_out) in enumerate(zip(sizes[:-1], sizes[1:]))] with m.dist.plate("sims", c.shape[0], subsample_size=batch_size) as idx: h = c[idx] for i, (W, bias) in enumerate(params): act = "gelu" if i < len(params) - 1 else None h = m.bnn.layer_linear(h, W, activation=act, bias=bias, verbose=False) # output layer: mixture weights, means and Cholesky factors -> likelihood of u m.bnn.layer_mixture_normal(h, K, D, diag_offset=0.5413, name="u", obs=u if u is None else u[idx]) ``` ::: ::: {#04cc2200 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} # 4. Train: point estimate of the weights with SVI, mini-batches of 256 simulations -- m.data_on_model = {"c": sn, "u": un, "batch_size": 256} m.svi(npe_net, guide=AutoDelta(npe_net, init_loc_fn=init_to_sample), optim=numpyro.optim.Adam(1e-3), loss=Trace_ELBO(), num_steps=20_000, num_samples=1000) ``` ::: ::: {#861ebd47 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} # 5. Posterior of the observed data: predictions of the trained network -------------- def npe_posterior(height, n=1000): c = (ols(height) - s_mean) / s_sd draws = m.sample(data={"c": c[None], "u": None, "batch_size": None}, samples=n)["u"][:, 0] return to_params(draws) npe_raw = npe_posterior(height_obs) for p in ["a", "b", "s"]: print(f"{p}: mean = {npe_raw[p].mean():.2f}, sd = {npe_raw[p].std():.2f}") # 6. Amortization: posteriors of the new datasets, no retraining ---------------------- npe_raw_new = [npe_posterior(h) for h in new_heights] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` a: mean = 154.58, sd = 0.34 b: mean = 5.93, sd = 0.40 s: mean = 5.05, sd = 0.27 ``` ::: ::: #### Built-in function The same analysis with `m.npe()`, which builds the training set from the model, handles the transforms and standardisation, and trains the same mixture density network; `m.npe_posterior()` reuses the trained network for new datasets. ::: {#9fcfaf8b .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Run NPE ------------------------------------------------ m.npe( model, data=howell, # the observed data (m.data_on_model now holds the training set) summary_stats=ols, estimator="mdn", # mixture density network num_simulations=20_000, progress_bar=False, ) # Summary ------------------------------------------------ m.summary() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}

jnp$matmul(X, coef)))) } # Run NPE ------------------------------------------------ m$npe(model, summary_stats = ols, estimator = "mdn", num_simulations = 20000L) # Summary ------------------------------------------------ m$summary() m$sbc_coverage(n_test = 200L) ``` ## Julia ```julia using BayesForge # Setup device------------------------------------------------ m = importBF(platform="cpu") # Import Data & Data Manipulation ------------------------------------------------ data_path = m.load.howell1(only_path = true) m.data(data_path, sep=';') m.df = m.df[m.df.age > 18] # Subset data to adults m.scale(["weight"]) # Normalize # Define model ------------------------------------------------ @BF function model(weight, height) a = m.dist.normal(178, 20, name = 'a') b = m.dist.log_normal(0, 1, name = 'b') s = m.dist.uniform(0, 50, name = 's') m.dist.normal(a + b * weight, s, obs = height) end # Summary statistics ------------------------------------------------ X = jnp.stack([jnp.ones(length(m.df.weight)), jnp.array(m.df.weight)], axis = 1) function ols(height) coef = jnp.linalg.lstsq(X, height)[1] jnp.stack([coef[1], coef[2], jnp.std(height - X * coef)]) end # Run NPE ------------------------------------------------ m.npe(model, summary_stats = ols, estimator = "mdn", num_simulations = 20_000) # Summary ------------------------------------------------ m.summary() m.sbc_coverage(n_test = 200) ``` ::: ## Mathematical Details ### *Model* The model is the linear regression of [chapter 1](1.%20Linear%20Regression%20for%20continuous%20variable.qmd): $$ Y_i \sim \text{Normal}(\alpha + \beta X_i, \sigma) $$ $$ \alpha \sim \text{Normal}(178, 20), \qquad \beta \sim \text{LogNormal}(0, 1), \qquad \sigma \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 50) $$ NPE only uses it to simulate datasets $Y_i = \alpha + \beta X_i + \sigma \varepsilon_i$, $\varepsilon_i \sim \text{Normal}(0, 1)$, summarised by the least-squares estimates $s(Y) = (\hat\alpha, \hat\beta, \hat\sigma)$, which are sufficient for this model. ### *Neural Posterior Estimation* NPE fits the network parameters $\phi$ by minimizing the expected negative log-density of the parameters that generated each simulated dataset: $$ \hat\phi = \arg\min_\phi \; \mathbb{E}_{\theta \sim p(\theta),\, x \sim p(x \mid \theta)}\left[-\log q_\phi\big(\theta \mid s(x)\big)\right] \approx \arg\min_\phi \; -\frac{1}{M}\sum_{j=1}^{M} \log q_\phi\big(\theta_j \mid s(x_j)\big) $$ This loss is the expected Kullback-Leibler divergence $\mathbb{E}_{p(x)}\big[\text{KL}\big(p(\theta \mid x)\,\|\,q_\phi(\theta \mid x)\big)\big]$ up to a constant, so it is minimized when $q_\phi(\theta \mid x) = p(\theta \mid x)$ for every $x$ [@papamakarios2016fast; @greenberg2019automatic]. This is why a single trained network is valid for all datasets (amortization). ### *Training set and transforms* `m.npe()` performs the following steps. 1. **Simulation.** $M$ pairs (`num_simulations`) are drawn from the prior predictive distribution, exactly as for ABC (see the [ABC chapter](38.%20Approximate%20Bayesian%20Computation.qmd)): $\theta_j \sim p(\theta)$, $x_j \sim p(x \mid \theta_j)$, $s_j = s(x_j)$. Pairs with non-finite values are dropped. 2. **Unconstrained parameters.** Each parameter is mapped to the real line by the bijection of its prior support, $u_j = T^{-1}(\theta_j)$ (here $u = (\alpha,\ \log\beta,\ \text{logit}(\sigma/50))$). The network models $q(u \mid s)$, so every sample $\theta = T(u)$ automatically respects the support. 3. **Standardisation.** Targets and inputs are standardised with the means and standard deviations of the training set: $\tilde u = (u - \bar u)/\text{sd}(u)$ and $\tilde s = (s - \bar s)/\text{sd}(s)$. The density of the original $u$ includes the Jacobian of this rescaling: $\log q(u \mid s) = \log \tilde q(\tilde u \mid \tilde s) - \sum_d \log \text{sd}(u_d)$. 4. **Training.** 10% of the pairs are held out for validation. The network is trained with Adam (learning rate `lr`) on mini-batches of `batch_size` pairs; every 200 steps the validation loss is computed, the best network so far is kept, and training stops when the validation loss has not improved for `patience` evaluations, or after `max_steps` steps. 5. **Posterior.** For the observed data, $\tilde s_{obs}$ is fed to the network, `num_samples` draws $\tilde u \sim \tilde q(\cdot \mid \tilde s_{obs})$ are un-standardised and mapped back with $\theta = T(u)$. `m.npe_posterior(x_new)` repeats this step for a new dataset, without new simulations. The from-scratch code trains the same network as a BF model. With Normal priors on the weights, $W^{(l)} \sim \text{Normal}(0, 1/\sqrt{n_{in}^{(l)}})$ and $b^{(l)} \sim \text{Normal}(0, 1)$, SVI with a point-mass guide (`AutoDelta`) finds the posterior mode of the weights, $$ \hat\phi = \arg\max_\phi \left[\sum_{j=1}^{M} \log q_\phi(u_j \mid s_j) + \log p(\phi)\right], $$ i.e. the NPE loss plus a weight decay ($\log p(\phi)$ is a sum of squared weights). Each SVI step uses a random mini-batch $B$ of 256 simulations (`m.dist.plate(..., subsample_size=256)`), whose log-likelihood is rescaled by $M/|B|$, for a fixed number of steps instead of early stopping. Posterior draws of a new dataset are predictions of the trained model: `m.sample()` runs the network on $\tilde s$ and draws $u$ from the mixture. ### *Mixture density network* (`estimator="mdn"`) $$ q_\phi(u \mid s) = \sum_{c=1}^{C} \pi_c(s)\; \text{MVNormal}\big(u \mid \mu_c(s),\, L_c(s) L_c(s)^\top\big) $$ Where: - $C$ is the number of mixture components (`n_components`), and $D$ the number of (scalar) parameters. - A multilayer perceptron (`hidden` layers of BF's `m.bnn.layer_linear`, activation `activation`) maps $\tilde s$ to $h(\tilde s) \in \mathbb{R}^{C(1 + D + D(D+1)/2)}$ (`m.bnn.mixture_normal_size(C, D)` outputs). - The output layer `m.bnn.layer_mixture_normal` splits $h$ into $C$ logits, $C$ means $\mu_c \in \mathbb{R}^D$ and $C$ vectors of $D(D+1)/2$ values, and returns the BF mixture distribution with weights $\pi_c = \text{softmax}(\text{logits})_c$. - Each vector of $D(D+1)/2$ values becomes a lower-triangular Cholesky factor with `m.bnn.layer_cholesky`: the values fill the lower triangle row by row and the diagonal is made positive, $L_{c,dd} = \text{softplus}(h_{c,dd} + \delta) + 10^{-3}$, so every covariance matrix $L_c L_c^\top$ is valid. With $\delta = 0.5413$ (used by `m.npe()` and the from-scratch code), the diagonal starts at 1, the scale of the standardised parameters; the weights of the output layer are also initialised 10 times smaller than the other layers, so training starts close to a mixture of standard Normal distributions. ### *Normalizing flow* (`estimator="flow"`) The flow transforms $u$ into a standard Normal variable $z$ through `n_layers` affine coupling layers [@dinh2017density]. Each layer uses a binary mask $m$ (alternating between layers) and keeps the masked coordinates unchanged: $$ u' = m \odot u + (1 - m) \odot \big(u \odot e^{a(m \odot u,\, h)} + b(m \odot u,\, h)\big) $$ where $a(\cdot)$ and $b(\cdot)$ are outputs of a multilayer perceptron that sees only the unchanged coordinates and an embedding $h$ of the summary statistics, and $a = 2\tanh(\cdot/2)$ is bounded for stability. The Jacobian of each layer is triangular, so the density is $$ \log q_\phi(u \mid s) = \log \text{Normal}(z \mid 0, I) + \sum_{\text{layers}} \sum_{d} (1 - m_d)\, a_d $$ and sampling inverts the layers in reverse order, $u = \big(u' - b\big) \odot e^{-a}$ on the transformed coordinates. ### *Expected coverage* For $n$ test pairs $(\theta^*_i, x^*_i)$ simulated from the model (`n_test`), `m.sbc_coverage()` draws $K$ samples $u_{ik} \sim q(\cdot \mid s(x^*_i))$ (`n_post`) and computes the mass of the smallest highest-density region that contains the true value: $$ r_i = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K} \mathbb{1}\left[q(u_{ik} \mid s_i) > q(u^*_i \mid s_i)\right] $$ The true value lies inside the $(1-\alpha)$ highest-density region when $r_i \le 1 - \alpha$, so the empirical coverage at level $1-\alpha$ is $\frac{1}{n}\sum_i \mathbb{1}[r_i \le 1 - \alpha]$ [@hermans2022trust]. A calibrated estimator has empirical coverage equal to $1-\alpha$ for every $\alpha$; a curve below the diagonal reveals over-confident posteriors, above the diagonal conservative ones. ## Notes ::: callout-note - NPE trades simulations for training: 20 000 simulations instead of the million used by ABC-SMC, but a network must be trained. It pays off when simulations are expensive or when many datasets must be analysed with the same model (amortization). - Two trainings of the same network (here `m.npe()` and the from-scratch code, which use the same settings but different random draws) give slightly different posteriors: over several seeds, both place the posterior means within about half an exact-posterior standard deviation of NUTS. This is the approximation error of a single trained network; more simulations reduce it. - An NPE posterior is only as good as the network fit. Always inspect the training curve (`m.sampler.plot_loss()`) and the expected coverage (`m.sbc_coverage()`) before interpreting the results. - The trained network is only valid for data similar to the simulations: observed data far outside the prior predictive distribution (model misspecification) give unreliable posteriors. - With a small simulation budget, use [Bayesian NPE](41.%20Bayesian%20Neural%20Posterior%20Estimation.qmd). ::: ## Reference(s) @papamakarios2016fast; @greenberg2019automatic; @cranmer2020frontier; @hermans2022trust ::: {#refs} :::
